bp: This record is a workshop proposal, so the object being built is not one new recommender algorithm. It is a forum for a field that has reached an uncomfortable handoff point. Online platforms already use recommendation and search to decide which products, articles, videos, songs, answers, or experiences a person sees. Older systems mostly learned from user-item interaction graphs: who clicked, bought, watched, skipped, or returned to what. The abstract says platforms now also hold richer evidence, including item text, visual content, audio signals, and metadata, while large language models and other semantic encoders can read that evidence in a more meaning-sensitive way. The workshop exists because these streams are colliding. Researchers and industry teams need to decide how generative models should fit beside conventional personalized systems, how they change knowledge discovery, and what future search and recommendation experiences should become.
wh: The hard part is that recommendation has never been only a language problem or only a click-prediction problem. User behavior shows what people actually did, but it can be sparse, biased by what the platform already showed, and silent about why a choice mattered. Text, images, audio, and metadata describe items more richly, but they do not by themselves prove that a specific user will want the item now. Generative models add another tension. They can produce explanations, synthetic descriptions, queries, or candidate suggestions, but generated text can sound plausible even when the underlying evidence is weak. Industrial adoption is growing while academic work is advancing quickly, which creates a coordination problem: systems may be deployed before the field has shared standards for how generative models and conventional recommenders should interact, be evaluated, and be trusted.
naive: A smart beginner might say: take a large language model, feed it the user's history and item descriptions, and ask it to recommend or explain. Another simple route would keep the old recommender unchanged and use the model only to decorate its results with friendlier text. Both are too shallow. The first route risks ignoring the hard-won behavioral signal in user-item graphs, because fluent semantic reasoning is not the same as knowing what users choose. The second route treats generative models as cosmetic wrappers, missing their possible role in candidate generation, knowledge discovery, personalization, and search. Neither route answers the workshop's real question: how should meaning-rich models and behavior-rich systems be combined responsibly?
ap: The core idea is to make the collision itself the subject of organized research discussion. The workshop bridges generative AI and recommender systems rather than treating one as a replacement for the other. Its central move is to gather work on the interplay between semantic encoders, large language models, visual and audio encoders, user-item interaction graphs, item content, metadata, search, and personalization. Mechanically, that means asking which parts of a personalized system should still come from conventional collaborative evidence, which parts can be improved by models that understand language or media, and where generation creates new risks. The abstract grounds the event as a third workshop, building on earlier forums, and expects a mixed academic and industrial audience. That matters because the open problem is partly technical and partly institutional: the field needs shared questions before it can converge on better systems.
mech: The input to this workshop is the current state of personalized platforms: interaction graphs connecting users to items, descriptions and media attached to users and items, metadata, and new generative or semantic models that can process those signals. The first transformation is conceptual sorting. Researchers bring examples where large language models, visual encoders, audio encoders, or generative methods change some part of search or recommendation. Those examples are compared with conventional personalized systems that already rank items from past behavior. The workshop then asks where the two kinds of evidence meet. One path may use semantic encoders to turn item text, images, or audio into comparable descriptions; another may use generation to produce candidate items, explanations, user profiles, or search experiences; another may study how these additions behave in industrial settings. The scoring is not a single benchmark number in the abstract. Instead, the workshop's mechanism is discussion across stakeholders: what capabilities are emerging, what research gap remains, what adoption pressures industry sees, and which future directions deserve attention. The output is expected to be shared understanding, research questions, and connections among more than 100 participants rather than a trained model or dataset.
math: The mathematical ideas are the familiar tools of recommendation, now under pressure from generation. Ranking is the first: from a large pile of possible items or search results, the system must produce a short order, and the order depends on what counts as useful for this user at this moment. Similarity is second: users, items, texts, images, and audio clips must be compared, so the system needs a way to decide which differences matter and which can be ignored. User-item interaction graphs add network reasoning: users and items are nodes, clicks or purchases are links, and links let evidence travel from one person's behavior to another possible item. Probability enters because every recommendation is uncertain; a click, purchase, or skip is only partial evidence of preference. Generative modeling adds controlled creation: instead of only choosing from a list, a system may produce text, explanations, user summaries, or candidates under the guidance of observed evidence. The tradeoff is compression versus meaning. Old systems compress behavior into scores; semantic models compress content into comparable descriptions; generation turns those compressed signals back into human-facing outputs, where mistakes can become persuasive.
dots: This workshop sits directly inside the repo's recommender-systems family, whose shared pressure is choosing a small useful set from a huge, changing pile while user intent, item meaning, cost, trust, and feedback loops all move. It also connects to the generative-diffusion family because the abstract frames generation as more than producing realistic samples: it may repair sparse evidence, create explanations, and shape personalized experiences. The ranking concept is central because search and recommendation still end in limited attention; only a few results can be shown. Similarity matters because semantic encoders try to compare item meaning across text, vision, audio, and metadata. Information matters because platforms must decide which signals are worth keeping, sharing, or spending computation on. The workshop's theme is therefore not a side topic. It names a broad 2026 field question: how should meaning-aware generation join behavior-based personalization?
ww: The workshop approach works if the field's difficulty is not merely missing a single technique, but missing a shared map of where techniques belong. The abstract supports that reading: it describes a confluence of data types, rapid advances in large language models and encoders, growing industrial adoption, and large questions about the future of personalized experiences. A normal paper can test one method against one task, but it cannot easily settle how search, recommendation, generation, semantic understanding, and deployment constraints should be connected across the field. Bringing academic and industrial participants together helps because each side sees a different failure mode. Academic researchers may see new modeling ideas before they are product-ready. Industrial teams see latency, scale, user trust, and adoption pressure. The workshop can improve over the naive approach by forcing these perspectives into the same room, so generative models are judged not just by fluency or novelty, but by how they interact with real behavioral evidence and existing personalized systems.
po: The payoff is agenda-setting rather than a direct performance gain. If successful, the workshop gives researchers and practitioners a common place to compare how generative models, semantic encoders, multimodal content signals, search, and conventional recommendation pipelines should fit together. The abstract claims the event will bridge a research gap and foster dialogue among academia and industry, with more than 100 expected attendees and key stakeholders. Grounded in the input, the practical capability it buys is coordination: clearer research questions, shared vocabulary, and faster movement from isolated generative-AI demos toward personalized systems that can use user behavior and content meaning together.
limits: Because this is a workshop proposal, the abstract does not prove a method, report controlled experiments, or show that any specific generative recommender improves user outcomes. Its value depends on the relevance of submitted work, the diversity of participants, and whether discussion turns into concrete research directions. It also assumes generative models and semantic encoders will remain important to recommendation and search, and that industrial adoption is broad enough to make coordination urgent. The abstract names large questions but does not specify evaluation standards, privacy safeguards, latency costs, hallucination controls, or how conventional and generative systems should be combined in deployment.
